title: How Paul Shaped His Letter to the Hebrews
english: From the preface: His way of instruction here is very wise indeed, and finely and skilfully crafted. It is woven from many strands: the writings of the law, spiritual insights, and the many-sided foretelling of the holy prophets. His aim is to teach at every point, and to persuade those who will read him, that the things given through Moses were types, in labor with the power of the truth, while the truth is Christ. So he shows that the proof by type and shadow, which the people of old so badly needed, is now superfluous. Besides this he makes something else plain to us: even those who lived splendidly under the law won good repute and approval in no other way than through faith in God, and faith is an ancient thing, well known to the holy fathers.

He did not use the openings and preambles that were his custom. For he was under suspicion and slander among the Jews who had believed, as a man who sided with those from the Gentiles and taught everyone everywhere to count the law as nothing, to despise the ancestral customs as worthless, and to take a different road, so to speak; this can be learned from the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 21:21). So with great tact he keeps his usual manner out of sight. He says nothing of the grace of his apostleship, and turns instead to the need to remember the fathers and the holy prophets, trusting that this would make his word easy for them to receive. So he said, "having spoken to the fathers in the prophets" (Hebrews 1:1).

God did speak to the people of earlier times in the Spirit, through the mouth of saints and the voice of prophets. Indeed, through one of them he said, to shame the senselessness of the Jews: "Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, will they live forever? But receive my statutes and my ordinances, all that I command by my Spirit to my servants the prophets" (Zechariah 1:5-6). Yet even if the grace of prophecy came to those of earlier times in the Spirit, it did not come apart from God the Word, who is from the Father; for his Spirit, in the same way, speaks to the saints. And surely no one with any sense would say that the Holy Spirit carries out a subordinate ministry toward us: that, like the prophets, he receives from God the Word the knowledge, or revelation, of whatever he may wish, and so passes it on to us. If that were so, he would differ in no way from the holy prophets. No: because he knows all that is in him, he is said to receive from him and to declare it to the saints (John 16:14). So it was the Only-begotten who spoke long ago as well, through the Holy Spirit, to the people of earlier times. translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74, Fragmenta in Hebraeos (Khazarzar PDF; text with Pusey's page numbers printed in it). Translated again clause by clause from the Greek on 11 Nov 2026; the earlier English was a summary.
The edition's Latin title lines are not printed; its heading "Fragment of the preface" is given as "From the preface:".
Zechariah 1:5-6 is quoted in the Septuagint's form ("receive my statutes"), which differs from the Hebrew.
The section stops mid-sentence where the source does; the quotation it introduces opens u01-rem-early.
